⏺ Rivers are among the oldest and most important features of the landscape, shaping valleys, carving canyons, and carrying water from highlands to the sea. Each one begins as a trickle from a spring,
  a melting glacier, or rain collecting on a mountainside, and grows as tributaries join it along the way. Over millennia, they erode rock, carry sediment, and build fertile floodplains where early
  civilizations settled. Rivers also serve as corridors for wildlife, supporting fish, birds, and plants along their banks. People have relied on them for drinking water, irrigation, transport, and
  power for thousands of years. Yet they are fragile, vulnerable to pollution, dams, and climate change. Protecting them means balancing human needs with the health of the ecosystems they sustain.
  Whether winding slowly through flat plains or tumbling over rapids in narrow gorges, every river tells a story of the land it crosses and the life it nourishes.
